name: Easter Island (Rapa Nui), Chile
clues: I am the loneliest crowd: nearly a thousand stone faces, and most of them turn their backs on the sea.
My nearest inhabited neighbor is more than 2,000 km of open ocean away.
Each spring, young men once swam to a rocky islet to bring back the first egg of the sooty tern.
Europeans named me after the holiday on which they arrived in 1722.
Giant carved heads called moai. Part of Chile, deep in the Pacific.
fact: Most moai face inland, watching over the villages that carved them.

name: Venice, Italy
clues: I have no cars, yet my streets are never empty of traffic.
I stand on millions of wooden piles driven into the mud of a lagoon.
Every year my ruler once 'married' the sea by throwing a gold ring into it.
More than 400 bridges cross my waters, and one of them is named for sighs.
The Italian city of gondolas and canals.
fact: The wooden piles under Venice have lasted centuries because, without oxygen underwater, they slowly turned almost to stone.

name: Timbuktu, Mali
clues: People say my name when they mean 'the middle of nowhere', yet I was once a capital of books.
Families here guarded hundreds of thousands of old manuscripts, and in 2012 many were smuggled out in rice sacks to save them.
My great mosques are made of mud and wood, and the whole town helps replaster them.
I sit near the Niger River, where camel caravans met river boats at the edge of the Sahara.
A legendary desert city in Mali whose name starts with 'Tim'.
fact: Timbuktu's Djinguereber Mosque was built around 1327 and is still made of mud brick.

name: Mount Everest
clues: I am still growing, a few millimeters every year.
Each spring a traffic jam forms where the air holds only a third of the oxygen you are breathing now.
I have three names: one honors a surveyor, one means 'goddess of the sky', one means 'holy mother'.
I sit on the border between Nepal and China.
The highest point on Earth above sea level.
fact: The summit of Everest is made of marine limestone. It was once the floor of an ancient sea.

name: Iguazu Falls, Argentina and Brazil
clues: A First Lady of the United States saw me and is said to have sighed: 'Poor Niagara!'
My name means simply 'big water'.
My loudest part is called the Devil's Throat.
I split my roar between two countries, and a third is only a few kilometers away.
Giant waterfalls on the Argentina and Brazil border.
fact: Iguazu is made of about 275 separate waterfalls spread over nearly 3 km.

name: Great Pyramid of Giza, Egypt
clues: For nearly 4,000 years I was the tallest thing humans had ever built.
Of the seven wonders on the ancient list, I am the only one still standing.
A lion with a human face keeps watch just below me.
I sit on a desert plateau at the edge of a megacity on the Nile.
The great pyramids just outside Cairo.
fact: The Great Pyramid was originally covered in polished white limestone that made it shine in the sun.

name: Svalbard (Longyearbyen), Norway
clues: I keep a doomsday library where the books are seeds.
Dying here is famously discouraged: the frozen ground will not let the dead decay.
Leave town without a rifle and you may meet a polar bear.
I am an Arctic archipelago governed by Norway, halfway to the North Pole.
Longyearbyen, the main town of Svalbard.
fact: The Global Seed Vault holds more than a million seed samples from almost every country.

name: Machu Picchu, Peru
clues: I was hidden so well in the clouds that the conquerors never found me.
My stones fit so tightly that a knife blade cannot slip between them, and no mortar holds them.
An explorer from Yale brought me to world fame in 1911.
I sit on a mountain ridge high above the Urubamba River.
The Inca citadel in the Andes of Peru.
fact: Machu Picchu was built in the 1400s, likely as an estate for the Inca emperor Pachacuti.

name: Uluru, Australia
clues: I change color with the sun: dusty brown at noon, glowing red at sunset.
I am one enormous block of sandstone, and most of me is hidden underground.
Climbing me was banned in 2019 out of respect for my traditional owners.
I stand alone in the Red Centre of a country that is also a continent.
Uluru, also called Ayers Rock.
fact: Uluru is about 348 m high and 9.4 km around at its base.

name: Salar de Uyuni, Bolivia
clues: After the rain I become the largest mirror on Earth.
I am so flat that satellites use me to check their measurements.
Some hotels here are built entirely out of me.
Under my crust lies a huge share of the world's lithium.
The biggest salt flat in the world, high in the Andes of Bolivia.
fact: Salar de Uyuni covers more than 10,000 square kilometers and varies in height by less than a meter.

name: Pripyat and Chernobyl, Ukraine
clues: A Ferris wheel here was set to open on May Day, but the crowds never came.
Wolves, lynx and wild horses now roam where 50,000 people once lived.
My clocks stopped in April 1986.
In 2016 a giant steel arch slid over my broken heart.
The abandoned city next to the Chernobyl nuclear plant.
fact: The New Safe Confinement arch over Chernobyl's reactor is one of the largest movable structures ever built.

name: Galapagos Islands, Ecuador
clues: A young man's five-week visit here in 1835 changed how we understand all of life.
Locals could tell which island a giant tortoise came from by the shape of its shell.
My iguanas swim in the sea and graze on seaweed.
I sit on the equator, about 1,000 km off the coast of South America.
The Galapagos Islands, part of Ecuador.
fact: Galapagos giant tortoises can live for more than 100 years.

name: Petra, Jordan
clues: A poet called me 'a rose-red city, half as old as time'.
My grandest building was never built. It was carved straight into the cliff.
You enter me through a narrow canyon called the Siq.
A movie archaeologist rode out of my Treasury in search of the Holy Grail.
The ancient Nabataean city of Petra.
fact: Scientists estimate that around 85% of Petra is still buried and unexcavated.

name: Victoria Falls, Zambia and Zimbabwe
clues: My local name means 'the smoke that thunders'.
My spray can be seen from 50 km away.
In the dry season, the bravest swim in a rock pool right at my edge.
A great river falls into a narrow gorge here, on the border of two countries.
Victoria Falls on the Zambezi River.
fact: At full flood, more than 500 million liters of water per minute pour over Victoria Falls.

name: Thingvellir, Iceland
clues: Here you can stand between two continents, and they are slowly pulling apart.
One of the world's oldest parliaments first met here, in the year 930.
Divers float in a crack in the earth, in water so clear they can see 100 meters.
I am a national park about an hour from the world's northernmost capital.
Thingvellir (Þingvellir), Iceland.
fact: The rift valley at Thingvellir widens by about 2 cm every year.

name: Angkor Wat, Cambodia
clues: My silhouette flies on my nation's flag.
I am the largest religious monument on Earth.
I was built for the god Vishnu, and later Buddhist monks moved in.
My towers rise from the jungle a few kilometers from Siem Reap.
Angkor Wat temple in Cambodia.
fact: Angkor Wat faces west, which is unusual for a temple of its kind, and the sun rises right behind its towers at the equinox.

name: Times Square, New York City
clues: Once a year a glowing ball falls here, and a million people stand in the cold to watch it.
I am named after a newspaper.
People call me the crossroads of the world.
Broadway cuts right through me.
Times Square, Manhattan.
fact: The New Year's Eve ball drop in Times Square started in 1907.

name: Lake Baikal, Russia
clues: I hold about a fifth of all the unfrozen fresh water on the planet.
The only seals that live only in fresh water swim in me.
I am the deepest and the oldest lake on Earth.
I lie in the middle of Siberia.
Lake Baikal.
fact: Lake Baikal is about 25 million years old and more than 1,600 m deep.

name: Socotra, Yemen
clues: My trees bleed red and look like umbrellas blown inside out.
A third of my plants grow nowhere else on Earth.
People call me the most alien-looking place on the planet.
I am an island where the Arabian Sea meets the Gulf of Aden.
Socotra island, part of Yemen.
fact: The red resin of Socotra's dragon's blood tree has been traded since ancient times as dye and medicine.

name: Christ the Redeemer, Rio de Janeiro
clues: My arms are 28 meters wide, and lightning strikes me several times a year.
I am covered in thousands of small triangles of soapstone.
I look down on a famous beach called Copacabana.
I stand on top of Corcovado mountain.
The Christ the Redeemer statue in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil.
fact: Christ the Redeemer was finished in 1931 and is about 30 m tall, not counting its pedestal.

name: The South Pole
clues: Stand here and every direction is north.
The sun rises once a year and sets once a year.
A striped barber pole topped with a mirrored ball marks me for photos.
Amundsen beat Scott here in 1911.
The southern end of Earth's axis.
fact: The ice at the South Pole moves about 10 m a year, so the marker for the exact pole is moved every January.

name: Great Blue Hole, Belize
clues: I am a perfect circle of darkness in a turquoise sea.
I was a dry cave until the ice age ended, the sea rose and swallowed my roof.
Jacques Cousteau named me one of the best dive sites in the world.
I lie on the second-largest barrier reef on Earth.
The Great Blue Hole, off the coast of Belize.
fact: The Great Blue Hole is about 300 m across and 125 m deep.

name: Pamukkale, Turkey
clues: I look like snow, but I am warm.
Water full of calcium built my white terraces, drop by drop.
An ancient Roman spa town sits right on top of me.
My name means 'cotton castle'.
Pamukkale, in southwestern Turkey.
fact: Visitors to Pamukkale must walk the terraces barefoot to protect the soft travertine.

name: Taj Mahal, India
clues: A grieving emperor built me for a wife who died giving birth to their 14th child.
My white marble turns pink at dawn and gold at sunset.
About 20,000 workers spent around 20 years building me.
I stand on the bank of the Yamuna River.
The Taj Mahal in Agra.
fact: The four minarets of the Taj Mahal lean slightly outward so they would fall away from the tomb in an earthquake.

name: Stonehenge, England
clues: Some of my stones were dragged about 240 km from the hills of Wales.
On the longest day of the year, the sun rises over my Heel Stone.
I am about 5,000 years old and I still keep my secrets.
I stand on a chalk plain in southern England.
Stonehenge, on Salisbury Plain.
fact: Stonehenge's biggest stones, the sarsens, weigh around 25 tonnes each.

name: Fushimi Inari Shrine, Kyoto, Japan
clues: Thousands of gates, and not a single door.
Each orange gate was donated by a person or a business hoping for good fortune.
Stone foxes guard my path. They are messengers of the god of rice.
I am in my country's old imperial capital.
Fushimi Inari shrine in Kyoto.
fact: The paths of torii gates at Fushimi Inari wind about 4 km up Mount Inari.

name: Point Nemo, South Pacific
clues: I am the place on Earth farthest from any land.
Often the closest humans to me are astronauts passing overhead.
Space agencies crash old spacecraft here on purpose. I am a spaceship graveyard.
I lie in the South Pacific Ocean.
The 'oceanic pole of inaccessibility', named after Jules Verne's submarine captain.
fact: The nearest land to Point Nemo is about 2,700 km away.

name: Great Wall of China (Badaling)
clues: Despite the famous myth, you cannot see me from the Moon with the naked eye.
I was built and rebuilt over 2,000 years by many dynasties.
A legend says a woman wept so hard for her husband that part of me collapsed.
My most visited section is about an hour from a capital city.
The Great Wall of China, at Badaling near Beijing.
fact: All the sections of the Great Wall added together stretch about 21,000 km.

name: Panama Canal, Panama
clues: I made some sea voyages about 13,000 km shorter overnight.
Ships here climb a staircase of water 26 meters high, then step back down.
Standing at my Pacific end, you can watch the sun rise over the Pacific.
I opened in 1914 and was handed over by the United States in 1999.
The canal across a narrow Central American country.
fact: Each ship passing through the Panama Canal uses about 200 million liters of fresh water from Gatun Lake.

name: Dead Sea
clues: I am the lowest place on dry land.
You cannot sink in me, but swimming is awkward.
Ancient scrolls were found in caves above my shore.
Jordan lies on my eastern shore.
A lake so salty it is called 'dead'.
fact: The Dead Sea's shore is about 430 m below sea level and the water level drops about 1 m a year.
